library(dplyr)

```{r , include=FALSE}
housing_confirmation <- read_csv(
  "housing_confirmation.csv",
  col_types = cols(
    id = col_character(),
    date = col_character(),
    zipcode = col_character(),
    grade_ = col_character()
  )
) %>%
  mutate(
    grade_ = factor(
      grade_,
      levels = c("7", "1-5", "6", as.character(8:11), "12-13")
    )
  )
```



```{r model-basic-grade, include=FALSE}
model_grade_only <- lm(
  log(price) ~ grade_,
  data = housing_confirmation
)

robust_grade_only <- coeftest(
  model_grade_only,
  vcov. = vcovHC(model_grade_only, type = "HC3")
)

robust_grade_only

cat("R-squared:", round(summary(model_grade_only)$r.squared, 4), "\n")
cat("Adjusted R-squared:", round(summary(model_grade_only)$adj.r.squared, 4), "\n")
cat("Observations:", nobs(model_grade_only), "\n")
```


```{r model-basic-sqft, include=FALSE}
model_sqft_living <- lm(
  log(price) ~ log(sqft_living) + I(log(sqft_living)^2),
  data = housing_confirmation
)

robust_sqft_living <- coeftest(
  model_sqft_living,
  vcov. = vcovHC(model_sqft_living, type = "HC3")
)

robust_sqft_living

cat("R-squared:", round(summary(model_sqft_living)$r.squared, 4), "\n")
cat("Adjusted R-squared:", round(summary(model_sqft_living)$adj.r.squared, 4), "\n")
cat("Observations:", nobs(model_sqft_living), "\n")
```



```{r model-complete, include=FALSE}
model_complete <- lm(
  log(price) ~ grade_ + log(sqft_living) +
    I(log(sqft_living)^2) + factor(zipcode),
  data = housing_confirmation
)

robust_complete <- coeftest(
  model_complete,
  vcov. = vcovHC(model_complete, type = "HC3")
)

robust_complete

cat("R-squared:", round(summary(model_complete)$r.squared, 4), "\n")
cat("Adjusted R-squared:", round(summary(model_complete)$adj.r.squared, 4), "\n")
cat("Observations:", nobs(model_complete), "\n")
```



# Introduction

Home sale prices vary substantially across properties, reflecting differences
in physical characteristics, construction quality, and geographic location.
Understanding how these factors are associated with home prices can provide
valuable insights for homebuyers, sellers, real estate professionals, and
other housing market participants.

While larger homes and homes with higher construction grades generally
command higher prices, these characteristics are also related to one another.
Furthermore, differences in geographic location may contribute substantially
to differences in home sale prices. Multiple regression allows these
relationships to be examined while controlling for other characteristics.

This study uses residential property sales in King County, Washington,
from May 28, 2014, to May 27, 2015, to address the following research questions.

## Research Questions

1. Is construction grade associated with home sale prices, controlling
   for living area and geographic location?

2. How is living area associated with home sale prices, controlling
   for construction grade and geographic location?

The objective of this study is to identify and quantify these associations
rather than establish causal relationships (experimentation realm) or develop a predictive model for home sale prices (machine learning realm).


# Research Question 1

***Is construction grade associated with home sale prices, controlling for
living area and geographic location?***

Construction grade exhibits a strong positive association with home sale prices. This relationship persists after controlling for living area and geographic location, although its magnitude is substantially reduced. Before adjustment, the estimated geometric mean sale price ranges from approximately $220,000 for Grades 1–5 to $2 million for Grades 12–13. After adjustment, this range narrows to approximately $375,000 to $850,000.

These findings suggest that differences in living area and geographic location account for a substantial portion of the unadjusted association. Nevertheless, higher construction grades remain positively and statistically significantly associated with home sale prices after accounting for these characteristics.

```{r grade-only-regression-plot, echo=FALSE, fig.width=9, fig.height=5}
grade_estimates <- emmeans(
  model_grade_only,
  ~ grade_,
  vcov. = vcovHC(model_grade_only, type = "HC3")
)

grade_plot_data <- as.data.frame(
  confint(grade_estimates, type = "response")
)

  grade_plot_unadjusted <- ggplot(
    grade_plot_data, aes(x = grade_, y = response)
  ) +
  geom_errorbar(
    aes(ymin = lower.CL, ymax = upper.CL),
    width = 0.15,
    color = "#38658D"
  ) +
  geom_point(size = 3, color = "#38658D") +
  scale_x_discrete(
    limits = c("1-5", "6", "7", as.character(8:11), "12-13")
  ) +
  scale_y_log10(
    labels = scales::label_dollar(),
    limits = c(200000, 2500000),
    breaks = c(200000, 300000, 500000, 1000000, 2000000)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Estimated Home Sale Price by Construction Grade",
    subtitle = "Unadjusted estimates with 95% robust confidence intervals",
    x = "Construction Grade",
    y = "Estimated Geometric Mean Sale Price (USD, log scale)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)
```


```{r complete-grade-plot, echo=FALSE, fig.width=9, fig.height=5}
mean_living_area <- mean(
  housing_confirmation$sqft_living,
  na.rm = TRUE
)

complete_grade_estimates <- emmeans(
  model_complete,
  ~ grade_,
  at = list(sqft_living = mean_living_area),
  nuisance = "zipcode",
  wt.nuis = "proportional",
  weights = "proportional",
  vcov. = vcovHC(model_complete, type = "HC3")
)

complete_grade_plot_data <- as.data.frame(
  confint(complete_grade_estimates, type = "response")
)

grade_plot_adjusted <- ggplot(
  complete_grade_plot_data,
  aes(x = grade_, y = response)
) +
  geom_errorbar(
    aes(ymin = lower.CL, ymax = upper.CL),
    width = 0.15,
    color = "#38658D"
  ) +
  geom_point(
    size = 3,
    color = "#38658D"
  ) +
  scale_x_discrete(
    limits = c("1-5", "6", "7", as.character(8:11), "12-13")
  ) +
  scale_y_log10(
    labels = scales::label_dollar(),
    limits = c(200000, 2500000),
    breaks = c(200000, 300000, 500000, 1000000, 2000000)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Adjusted Relationship Between Construction Grade and Home Sale Price",
    subtitle = paste0(
      "Controlling for living area (",
      scales::comma(round(mean_living_area)),
      " sq. ft.) and ZIP code"
    ),
    x = "Construction Grade",
    y = "Estimated Geometric Mean Sale Price (USD, log scale)",
    caption = paste(
      "ZIP codes weighted by sample proportions.",
      "Error bars represent 95% robust confidence intervals.",
      sep = "\n"
    )
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)
```

```{r grade-plots-combined, echo=FALSE, fig.width=11, fig.height=5}
patchwork::wrap_plots(
  grade_plot_unadjusted +
    labs(
      title = "Unadjusted",
      subtitle = NULL,
      caption = NULL
    ),
  grade_plot_adjusted +
    labs(
      title = "Adjusted",
      subtitle = NULL,
      caption = NULL
    ),
  ncol = 2,
  axes = "collect_y",
  axis_titles = "collect"
) +
  patchwork::plot_annotation(
    title = "Relationship Between Construction Grade and Home Sale Price",
    caption = paste(
      paste0(
        "Adjusted estimates hold living area constant at ",
        scales::comma(round(mean_living_area)),
        " sq. ft., with ZIP codes weighted by sample proportions."
      ),
      "Error bars represent 95% robust confidence intervals.",
      sep = "\n"
    )
  )
```



# Research Question 2

***How is living area associated with home sale prices, controlling for
construction grade and geographic location?***

Living area exhibits a positive, nonlinear association with home sale prices. This relationship persists after controlling for construction grade and geographic location, although both the steepness and curvature of the relationship are substantially reduced.

The quadratic coefficient decreases from 0.39 to 0.14 after adjustment, representing an approximately 65% reduction in curvature on the log-log scale. Nevertheless, the quadratic term remains statistically significant, indicating that the percentage increase in estimated sale price associated with a given percentage increase in living area is greater for larger homes.

These findings suggest that differences in construction grade and geographic location partially account for the strong nonlinear relationship observed before adjustment.

```{r living-area-plot-preparation, include=FALSE}
log_scatter_data <- housing_confirmation %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(price),
    !is.na(sqft_living),
    price > 0,
    sqft_living > 0
  )

# Shared living area range
living_area_range <- quantile(
  log_scatter_data$sqft_living,
  probs = c(0.01, 0.99),
  na.rm = TRUE
)

sqft_grid <- exp(seq(
  log(living_area_range[1]),
  log(living_area_range[2]),
  length.out = 500
))

# Unadjusted estimates
sqft_living_estimates <- emmeans(
  model_sqft_living,
  ~ sqft_living,
  at = list(sqft_living = sqft_grid),
  vcov. = vcovHC(model_sqft_living, type = "HC3")
)

sqft_living_plot_data <- as.data.frame(
  confint(sqft_living_estimates, type = "response")
)

# Adjusted estimates
complete_living_estimates <- emmeans(
  model_complete,
  ~ sqft_living,
  at = list(sqft_living = sqft_grid),
  nuisance = c("grade_", "zipcode"),
  wt.nuis = "proportional",
  weights = "proportional",
  vcov. = vcovHC(model_complete, type = "HC3")
)

complete_living_plot_data <- as.data.frame(
  confint(complete_living_estimates, type = "response")
)

# Shared axis limits
living_area_x_limits <- range(
  log_scatter_data$sqft_living,
  na.rm = TRUE
)

living_area_y_limits <- range(
  c(
    log_scatter_data$price,
    sqft_living_plot_data$lower.CL,
    sqft_living_plot_data$upper.CL,
    complete_living_plot_data$lower.CL,
    complete_living_plot_data$upper.CL
  ),
  na.rm = TRUE
)
```


```{r sqft-living-log-log-plot, echo=FALSE, fig.width=9, fig.height=6}
living_area_plot_unadjusted <- ggplot() +
  geom_point(
    data = log_scatter_data,
    aes(x = sqft_living, y = price),
    alpha = 0.16,
    size = 0.7,
    color = "#38658D"
  ) +
  geom_ribbon(
    data = sqft_living_plot_data,
    aes(x = sqft_living, ymin = lower.CL, ymax = upper.CL),
    fill = "#C05A46",
    alpha = 0.20
  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = sqft_living_plot_data,
    aes(x = sqft_living, y = response),
    color = "#C05A46",
    linewidth = 1
  ) +
  scale_x_log10(
    labels = scales::label_comma(),
    limits = living_area_x_limits
  ) +
  scale_y_log10(
    labels = scales::label_dollar(),
    limits = living_area_y_limits
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Unadjusted Relationship Between Living Area and Sale Price",
    subtitle = "Quadratic log-log regression without controls",
    x = "Living Area (Sq. Ft., log scale)",
    y = "Home Sale Price (USD, log scale)",
    caption = paste(
      "Points represent observed home sale prices.",
      "Fitted curve represents the estimated geometric mean sale price.",
      "Fitted curve restricted to the 1st–99th percentiles of living area.",
      "Shaded region represents the 95% robust confidence interval.",
      sep = "\n"
    )
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)
```

# Models

The primary variables of interest, construction grade and living area, both exhibit statistically significant associations with home sale prices. Among the additional property characteristics evaluated during exploration, ZIP code provided the only meaningful improvement in descriptive power and was therefore included to account for geographic differences in home sale prices.

The complete model incorporates a quadratic log-log specification for living area to capture the nonlinear relationship between living area and home sale price.


```{r stargazer-combined, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
stargazer(
  model_grade_only,
  model_sqft_living,
  model_complete,
  type = "latex",
  title = "Association Between Housing Characteristics and Home Sale Price",
  dep.var.labels = "Log of Home Sale Price",
  column.labels = c(
    "Grade Only",
    "Living Area Only",
    "Complete Model"
  ),
  covariate.labels = c(
    "Grade 1-5",
    "Grade 6",
    "Grade 8",
    "Grade 9",
    "Grade 10",
    "Grade 11",
    "Grade 12-13",
    "Log of Living Area",
    "Squared Log of Living Area"
  ),
  se = list(
    robust_grade_only[, 2],
    robust_sqft_living[, 2],
    robust_complete[, 2]
  ),
  t = list(
    robust_grade_only[, 3],
    robust_sqft_living[, 3],
    robust_complete[, 3]
  ),
  p = list(
    robust_grade_only[, 4],
    robust_sqft_living[, 4],
    robust_complete[, 4]
  ),
  t.auto = FALSE,
  p.auto = FALSE,
  omit = "factor\\(zipcode\\)",
  add.lines = list(
    c("ZIP Code Fixed Effects", "No", "No", "Yes")
  ),
  digits = 4,
  keep.stat = c("n", "rsq", "adj.rsq"),
  notes = "HC3 robust standard errors in parentheses. Reference: Grade 7.",
  font.size = "small",
  table.placement = "H",
  header = FALSE
)
```



\clearpage

# Model Fit and Diagnostics

The predicted and actual home sale prices exhibit close agreement, with most
observations concentrated around the 45-degree reference line, indicating a strong
overall model fit. However, the model tends to overestimate the prices of some
lower-priced homes and underestimate the prices of some higher-priced homes.

```{r complete-model-predicted-actual, echo=FALSE, fig.width=8, fig.height=7, out.width="50%", fig.align="center"}
predicted_actual_data <- tibble(
  actual_log_price = model.response(model.frame(model_complete)),
  predicted_log_price = fitted(model_complete)
) %>%
  mutate(
    actual_price = exp(actual_log_price),
    predicted_price = exp(predicted_log_price)
  )

price_range <- range(
  c(
    predicted_actual_data$actual_price,
    predicted_actual_data$predicted_price
  )
)

ggplot(
  predicted_actual_data,
  aes(x = actual_price, y = predicted_price)
) +
  geom_point(
    alpha = 0.16,
    size = 0.7,
    color = "#38658D"
  ) +
  geom_abline(
    intercept = 0,
    slope = 1,
    color = "#C05A46",
    linetype = "dashed",
    linewidth = 1
  ) +
  scale_x_log10(
    labels = scales::label_dollar(),
    limits = price_range
  ) +
  scale_y_log10(
    labels = scales::label_dollar(),
    limits = price_range
  ) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(
    title = "Predicted vs. Actual Home Sale Prices",
    subtitle = "Complete quadratic regression model; confirmation sample",
    x = "Actual Sale Price (USD, log scale)",
    y = "Predicted Sale Price (USD, log scale)",
    caption = paste(
      "Dashed line represents perfect agreement.",
      "Fitted values represent estimated geometric mean sale prices.",
      sep = "\n"
    )
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)
```



The residuals are generally centered around zero, with the LOESS trend line
remaining relatively flat across the range of fitted values. This suggests that the
model adequately captures the overall functional relationship between the
explanatory variables and log sale price. While some variation in residual
dispersion is observed, there is no pronounced pattern of heteroskedasticity.
Nevertheless, heteroskedastic robust standard errors are used to ensure more
reliable statistical inference.

```{r complete-model-residuals-vs-fitted, echo=FALSE, fig.width=9, fig.height=5, out.width="50%", fig.align="center"}
residual_data <- tibble(
  fitted_log_price = fitted(model_complete),
  residual = residuals(model_complete)
)

ggplot(residual_data, aes(x = fitted_log_price, y = residual)) +
  geom_point(
    alpha = 0.16,
    size = 0.7,
    color = "#38658D"
  ) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = 0,
    linetype = "dashed",
    color = "gray40"
  ) +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "loess",
    formula = y ~ x,
    se = FALSE,
    color = "#C05A46",
    linewidth = 1
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Residuals vs. Fitted Values",
    subtitle = "Complete quadratic regression model; confirmation sample",
    x = "Fitted Log Sale Price",
    y = "Residual (Log Scale)",
    caption = paste(
      "Red curve represents the LOESS trend in residuals.",
      "Dashed line represents zero residual.",
      sep = "\n"
    )
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)
```




# Methodology

## Satisfying Large Sample Linear Regression Model Requirements

### 1. Independent and Identically Distributed (IID)

Independence of home sale price data is plausible, but not perfect. Home sellers
typically benchmark prices of homes sold in their area so there would be some geographic clustering effect because of this. Also, there are times although probably less often when someone would sell their home in King County then would buy a home also in King County. When this happens, how much they sell their may carry some information on how much they would buy their next home.

### 2. A Unique Best Linear Predictor (BLP) Exists

**a. No Infinite Variance**

Sales price and living area both have heavy right tails indicating possible
inifinite variance. To eliminate the heavy tail, a log transform is performed.

```{r price-distributions, echo=FALSE, fig.width=10, fig.height=4.5}
price_distribution_data <- housing_confirmation %>%
  filter(!is.na(price), price > 0) %>%
  mutate(log_price = log(price))

# Original price distribution
price_plot_raw <- ggplot(price_distribution_data, aes(x = price)) +
  geom_histogram(
    bins = 35,
    fill = "#4472A5",
    color = "white"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_dollar()) +
  labs(
    title = "Home Sale Price",
    x = "Sale Price (USD)",
    y = "Number of Homes"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)

# Log-transformed price distribution
price_plot_log <- ggplot(price_distribution_data, aes(x = log_price)) +
  geom_histogram(
    bins = 35,
    fill = "#4472A5",
    color = "white"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Log of Home Sale Price",
    x = "Log Sale Price",
    y = "Number of Homes"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)

# Combine charts with shared title and caption
patchwork::wrap_plots(
  price_plot_raw,
  price_plot_log,
  ncol = 2
) +
  patchwork::plot_annotation(
    title = "Distribution of Home Sale Prices",
    caption = "Confirmation sample"
  )
```


```{r living-area-distributions, echo=FALSE, fig.width=10, fig.height=4.5}
living_area_distribution_data <- housing_confirmation %>%
  filter(!is.na(sqft_living), sqft_living > 0) %>%
  mutate(log_sqft_living = log(sqft_living))

# Original living area distribution
living_area_plot_raw <- ggplot(
  living_area_distribution_data, aes(x = sqft_living)
) +
  geom_histogram(
    bins = 35,
    fill = "#4472A5",
    color = "white"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(
    title = "Living Area",
    x = "Living Area (Sq. Ft.)",
    y = "Number of Homes"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)

# Log-transformed living area distribution
living_area_plot_log <- ggplot(
  living_area_distribution_data, aes(x = log_sqft_living)
) +
  geom_histogram(
    bins = 35,
    fill = "#4472A5",
    color = "white"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Log of Living Area",
    x = "Log Living Area",
    y = "Number of Homes"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)

# Combine charts with shared title and caption
patchwork::wrap_plots(
  living_area_plot_raw,
  living_area_plot_log,
  ncol = 2
) +
  patchwork::plot_annotation(
    title = "Distribution of Living Area",
    caption = "Confirmation sample"
  )
```

**b. No perfect collinearity between X variables**

There is no perfect collinearity between construction grade, living area, and zip
code as they are all showing up as statistically significant variables in the
complete model.


## Heteroskedastic Robust Standard Errors

Used the heteroskedastic robust standard errors (HC3) so that the homoskedastic
error assumption of the classical linear regression model would not have to be
satisfied. Because of the large sample size (~14,000), the loss of power resulting
from using heteroskedastic standard errors is minimized.


## Exploration and Confirmation Samples

To reduce the risk of false-positive findings arising from data-driven model
selection, data exploration and model development were performed on a randomly
selected 30% of the approximately 20,000 observations. The remaining 70% were used
to estimate the selected regression models and assess whether the findings from the
exploration sample persisted.


# APPENDIX

## Correlation Matrix

```{r confirmation-correlation-matrix, echo=FALSE, fig.width=8, fig.height=6}
correlation_variables <- c(
  "price",
  "grade",
  "sqft_living",
  "sqft_lot",
  "age",
  "condition",
  "renovated"
)

correlation_data <- housing_confirmation %>%
  select(all_of(correlation_variables))

correlation_matrix <- cor(
  correlation_data,
  method = "spearman",
  use = "complete.obs"
)

# Prepare data for heatmap
correlation_plot_data <- as.data.frame(
  as.table(correlation_matrix)
)

colnames(correlation_plot_data) <- c(
  "Variable1", "Variable2", "Correlation"
)

# Report-friendly variable labels
correlation_labels <- c(
  price = "Sale Price",
  grade = "Construction Grade",
  sqft_living = "Living Area",
  sqft_lot = "Lot Area",
  age = "Age",
  condition = "Condition",
  renovated = "Renovated"
)

ggplot(
  correlation_plot_data,
  aes(x = Variable1, y = Variable2, fill = Correlation)
) +
  geom_tile(color = "white") +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", Correlation)),
    size = 3.5
  ) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    low = "#38658D",
    mid = "white",
    high = "#B35806",
    midpoint = 0,
    limits = c(-1, 1),
    name = "Spearman \u03c1"
  ) +
  scale_x_discrete(
    limits = correlation_variables,
    labels = correlation_labels
  ) +
  scale_y_discrete(
    limits = rev(correlation_variables),
    labels = correlation_labels
  ) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(
    title = "Correlations Among Key Housing Variables",
    subtitle = "Spearman rank correlation",
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL,
    caption = "Confirmation sample"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
    panel.grid = element_blank()
  )
```
